content:
Elliot Price: hey docs folks — for the model changelog/release notes, we need crisp wording guidelines. main goal: be transparent but *do not* leak internal model nicknames or vendor specifics. can we align today on a do/don’t list + a default template?

Wei Chen: +1. we’ve already got a few draft notes that say things like “sunfish build” 😬 we should explicitly ban internal codenames.

Kira Thompson: also ban vendor + infra breadcrumbs. enterprise customers will paste these into change mgmt systems and we don’t want to accidentally disclose hardware/provider changes (esp for Private).

Marissa Cole: product POV: customers want “what changed + should I do anything + can I roll back”. they *don’t* need implementation details. we can be specific on impact/compatibility and stay vague on underlying cause.

Elliot Price: cool. here’s what I’m thinking for “don’t leak”:
- no internal model nicknames/codenames
- no internal incident IDs / jira links / slack links
- no vendor-specific kernel/driver details
- no internal benchmark names

Wei Chen: :thumbsup: also “no cluster names / region nicknames” (we have those weird internal names that are definitely not customer-safe)

Dylan Brooks: +1 and we should treat it as a hard requirement in the generator. even if someone types it, it should get flagged/redacted. we’re adding an allowlist of public fields on the registry side — but docs copy still needs rules.

Paula Mendes: question: can we mention “runtime upgrade” if it affects throughput? or is that too close to vendor/infra?

Kira Thompson: “runtime upgrade” is fine, but not “upgraded to CUDA X / driver Y / H100 kernel path” etc. phrase it like “inference engine update” or “serving stack update” and then talk in terms of observed impact.

Wei Chen: agreed. maybe:
- OK: “Serving stack update improved median latency by ~8% on typical workloads.”
- NOT OK: “Enabled FlashAttention2 on H100s in us-east-1a”

Elliot Price: :100: also we should avoid “we changed batching params” unless it’s a customer-facing knob.

Jada Williams: on the workflow side, we can enforce a required “Customer-visible summary” field that gets linted. if it includes banned tokens (codename list, gpu terms, vendor list), we fail the draft -> in_review transition.

Dylan Brooks: yep. for banned tokens we can start with a simple list (codenames, internal project names, cloud provider names) and expand. also note: some model providers are fine to mention (e.g. “Llama 3”) but some partner models are under NDA — we need a per-model “public_name” vs “internal_name”.

Wei Chen: can we align on canonical naming in the doc copy? i’d propose:
- “Model”: use the customer-facing model name from catalog
- “Version”: use Redwood version id (e.g. `2026-02-15`) or `version_id`
- never mention upstream repo hash / build id

Marissa Cole: yes. and always include: “How to pin / how to roll back” link if applicable.

Elliot Price: template proposal (per entry):
1) Summary (1–2 sentences)
2) Impact (perf/behavior)
3) Compatibility (API params, tool/function calling, context length)
4) Actions (if any)
5) Deprecation (if any) w/ dates
6) Links (docs + console) — no internal dashboards

Kira Thompson: add “Deployment availability” line too: Hosted/Dedicated/Private. customers keep asking “is this change in my env?”

Paula Mendes: +1. and on rollouts pages we’re going to show “Published for Hosted” and later “Enabled in your rollout”. so wording should not imply everyone got it already.

Wei Chen: we should standardize verbs:
- “Available” = can be selected/pinned
- “Default” = used when customers specify the base model without version pin
- “Rolled out” = actually applied to default traffic (and usually gradual)

Elliot Price: good call. we’ve had notes that said “released” and customers assumed their default changed.

Dylan Brooks: another gotcha: don’t mention “fallback happened” or “capacity tier routing” details. we can say “improved reliability under load” but not describe routing policy.

Kira Thompson: and for security/compliance, avoid “we saw customer X” anecdotes. if we need to reference cause, use generic language: “addresses an issue where some requests could…”

Wei Chen: what about quality changes? we said v1 won’t do full narrative from eval diffs, but sometimes we need to say “fixed hallucination regression” etc.

Marissa Cole: we can say “Behavior: reduced incorrect tool calls in some cases” but avoid claiming “more accurate” unless we have evidence + scope. also no “we changed training data” type claims.

Elliot Price: maybe a safe pattern:
- “No observed regressions on Redwood standard eval suite; see linked metrics.”
- If there is a known tradeoff, state it plainly + mitigation.

Dylan Brooks: careful with the eval link too. we can link to a customer-safe page (console or docs) that shows aggregate metrics. not internal eval set names like “orca-math-23” etc.

Wei Chen: yep, use “Redwood standard eval suite” and “selected prompts” as generic terms. also avoid raw prompt content if it’s licensed.

Kira Thompson: enterprise angle: deprecation messaging needs to be super explicit:
- date when new deployments are blocked
- date when existing pins stop serving
- replacement model/version
and avoid “end of quarter” language. always actual dates.

Paula Mendes: +1. we’ve had customers require 90 days notice. we should bake that into wording and the generator can check it.

Jada Williams: workflow note: we can add a required “Deprecation notice period (days)” field and validate against policy before publish.

Elliot Price: ok, action items:
- Wei: draft a do/don’t section + example “bad vs good” phrases
- Kira: add enterprise-specific language guidance (deprecation + audit-friendly wording)
- I’ll update the docs style guide page + send to Marissa/Dylan for sign-off

Wei Chen: sounds good. I’ll include a banned examples list:
- codenames (“sunfish”, “orca”, “paperclip”)
- vendors (“NVIDIA”, “AWS”, “GCP”, “Azure”) unless explicitly approved
- hardware (“H100”, “A100”, “CUDA”, “driver”, “kernel”)
- internal systems (“grafana”, “honeycomb”, “SIEM export job name”)

Dylan Brooks: (small nuance) “AWS/GCP/Azure” might be ok in general docs, but for model release notes specifically I’d rather keep it provider-neutral. +1 to banning by default.

Marissa Cole: thank you. also please add: always include compatibility notes even if “no change”. support keeps getting tickets where customers ask “did tool calling change?” and we have no line item.

Elliot Price: got it. will make “Compatibility” a required section, with explicit “No changes” allowed.

Kira Thompson: and a final “Confidentiality” check: if a note contains anything that implies supplier relationships, route to compliance reviewer. we can keep it lightweight but it should exist.

Jada Williams: we can tag entries “sensitive_review_required=true” based on model/provider metadata and require Marcus/Naomi sign-off.

Elliot Price: perfect. I’ll bake that into the guideline doc and the checklist. :thumbsup:
